text:
Can you write an email to people who didn't renew their farm share? I run a 30-acre vegetable farm and sell 22-week shares that people pick up every Thursday.

Facts:
- Last year 260 households had a share. 97 didn't renew.
- On July 9 a hailstorm destroyed about half our crops. For the next 6 weeks the boxes had about half the usual amount. We didn't offer refunds or credit, and I sent one short email about it.
- A full share is $540 this year, the same as last year.
- This year we've added a second field on higher ground and put up 2 hail nets over our tomatoes and peppers. That cost $31,000.
- Members can now pause up to 2 weeks and get credit for them.
- Sign-up closes March 15. 52 shares are left.

Under 200 words.

Before I draft, a few questions. Your answers will change what the email says:

1. **How much do you want to own last summer?** You gave no refund or credit and sent one short email. I'd suggest saying plainly that you handled it badly. Are you comfortable with that, or would you rather just acknowledge the storm?
2. **Do you know why these 97 left?** For example, did people reply, complain, or mention the hail? If most left for other reasons (they moved, had too much produce, the price), the email should lead with something else.
3. **Can you offer anything to returning members?** Some options are a small discount, a free week, or credit toward last year's short boxes. If not, that's fine. I'll make the case using the field, the nets and the new pause option.
4. **Would the new field and nets have saved what you lost in July?** For instance, were the lost crops mostly tomatoes and peppers, or crops in low-lying ground? I want to claim only what's true.
5. **What are the farm name, your sign-off name and the sign-up link?**

1. Yes, I want to say sorry plainly. I didn't write more because I was working 16-hour days trying to save what was left, but I handled it badly.

2. 41 of the 97 answered a short survey in the fall. 29 of them said they'd come back if we fixed how we handle bad weeks.

3. No discount or free week. But I can commit to a credit for any week when weather cuts a box by more than a third. I can also send a short email to members every Thursday of the season.

4. I don't know exactly what share of the loss was tomatoes and peppers. The nets only cover tomatoes and peppers, not the greens, and I can't promise there won't be crop loss this year.

5. Greenbank Farm, Sam Turner. Sign-up is through the link on our website.

<final_document>
Subject: I handled last summer badly

Hi [first name],

After the July 9 hailstorm, your box was about half its usual size for six weeks. I didn't offer a refund or credit, and I sent you one short email. I was working 16-hour days to save what was left, but that's no excuse. You deserved better, and I'm sorry.

Most of you who answered our fall survey said you'd come back if we fixed how we handle bad weeks. Here's what's changed:

- If weather cuts a box by more than a third, you get credit for that week.
- I'll send a short email every Thursday of the season, so you'll always know what's happening on the farm.
- You can pause up to two weeks and get credit for them.

We've also spent $31,000 on a second field on higher ground and two hail nets over the tomatoes and peppers. The nets don't cover the greens, and I can't promise a season without loss. But if something goes wrong, you'll hear from me.

A full share is still $540. Sign-up closes March 15, and 52 shares are left. Sign up through the link on our website.

I'd love to have you back.

Sam Turner
Greenbank Farm
</final_document>

The email is about 195 words, not counting the subject line. It starts with the apology because that's what your survey says will bring people back: 29 of the 41 who answered said they'd return if you fixed how you handle bad weeks. That's why the weather credit and the Thursday emails come before the new field and the nets.

I said "most of you who answered" rather than giving the exact numbers because it reads more warmly. I also kept the line about the nets not covering greens, so nobody can say later that you promised more than you could deliver.

Please put in the real website link if you can. A direct link to the sign-up page will get more people to sign up than "the link on our website."
